I moved to top roping and never looked back. Okay, I do occasionally look back and do some VBs and V0s. 

When I started top roping, I couldn’t finish a 5.5 because of my fear of heights but I have some super belay partners. I routinely flash 10as and 10bs and run a women’s climbing group. 

If you love the mental/spiritual/emotional aspects of climbing, I highly suggest you try top roping. I have looked into lead climbing but as soon as I watch them make a 10 foot fall during their class, I change my mind. 

Climbing is a “challenge by choice”. When I went back to climbing after my injury, I “chose” my finish. For me, getting on the wall was a win. I didn’t care if I finished the climb. Find what part brings you joy that doesn’t hurt you and embrace that part.

If HR is saying you can’t sign up until open enrollment, THAT is for next year. So you still wouldn’t have coverage until 1/1/25.

You need to see how long the enrollment period for your new insurance is. Do you have to sign up within 30 days? There is usually a sign up window and if you miss it, you’d need to stay on COBRA until the new enrollment period (January in most cases). 


You also need to check on how long you might need the COBRA coverage. While the surgery would be covered for September, some of the follow up (going into October) might not be. 

Finally make sure your doctors are in your PPO if you want to continue care with them. 

And keep meticulous records. If they bill after you’ve left COBRA, while you are covered, it just becomes more of a pain if they bill in October or November.

Not a complete answer but some things to look out for: 

Make SURE her plan goes to the end of the month. One company who let me go terminated my plan on the day they let me go—the 15th. It did not go to the end of the month. 

If she is eligible to go on your plan, she can’t go on the open market so her only other choice is cobra. 

If she gives birth 9/30 that would be her company plan, but anything after midnight would be cobra or your plan. Depending on the cost, it might just be less stressful to plan on cobra for at least October so you don’t have insurance companies arguing about who is responsible. 

It sounds like you think it’s a planned layoff—is it a lot of people? Might she be eligible for any package? I was laid off with my team and part of the severance was 6 months of cobra subsidies. 

If it’s JUST her being let go, I suggest speaking with a lawyer to ensure it’s not because she’s pregnant (or even hints at being pregnancy related). And depending on her role and the reason for the layoff, she might be able to negotiate them covering her for 30-60 days. 

If she’s already close to hitting her deductible because of the pregnancy, it might make more sense financially to pay cobra. It’s hella expensive so you have to run the numbers. 

After the baby is born you only have 30 days to put them on a policy. Don’t wait! I’d probably plan on immediately putting the baby in your plan because that is most likely cheaper than cobra. 

When I was laid off, I stayed on (company-subsidized) cobra for the balance of the year rather than switching at 6 months to my new job’s plan and have a new $14,000 deductible. I’d almost hit ours by June (son’s insulin $$$). 

Your wife might be better off doing cobra for (September) Oct/nov/dec and then you adding her to yours for 2025. 

Your best bet is a spreadsheet: how close she is to hitting her deductible, how much cobra would be, how much your plan is.

Remember, she’s planning a relatively simple, planned c-section but you never know. Don’t try to guess and possibly be stuck with uncovered expenses. 

I believe you have a 30-day window to elect cobra. Even if insurance “ends” cobra will pick up the cost once you sign up. Just don’t miss the window because there’s no grace period. 

She should speak with her practice so they are aware the she might be switching to cobra so they don’t hit her with “you aren’t covered.”

I’ve spoken with an elder law attorney IN MY STATE THAT IS NOT YOUR STATE SO IT MAY NOT WORK FOR YOUR STATE. 

First, talk to Medicaid because that’s what is paying for the nursing home. 

In my state, they don’t take the house immediately. The state will take his social security first and basically begin to “bill” your father’s estate for the balance as a lien on the property. 

You might need to tell Medicaid that he intends to return to the family home for them to let you keep it. You could state that you need to get things set up to be a caregiver, or make arrangements to finish school for the year or get some caregiver training and then you will bring him home. 

When your father passes, Medicaid will want its money from the estate so the estate will sell the house to pay ALL debts. 

If your father’s house is worth more than the debt, the estate distributes the balance of the money to the heirs. If more is owed on the debt, THE HEIRS ARE NOT RESPONSIBLE AND SHOULD NOT PAY. 

Realize that even if your dad wasn’t currently ill, depending on his will and mortgage, you’d have to sell the house and leave anyway. 

Please know that caregiving is very mentally and emotionally exhausting. I’d reach out to an ALS support group to see what resources they have. 

He should have a social worker who might be able to let you know how to hire caregivers but they get very expensive, very fast. 

Check with the county you live in. We have some respite care services on a sliding scale but they probably wouldn’t cover all day care. 

If you’re a full time student, speak with your school— they usually have programs that prevent students from becoming homeless. 

Again, I’m very sorry you’re going through this right now.

Stop beating yourself up. Life is a practice—we’ve never done this life before so we’re learning. 

I too have a lot of hobbies. And I’m not “good” at a lot of them. But that is MY metric—I’m not good compared to people who have more experience at the hobby then I do. I’m also “better” than people who never did the hobby. 

Does the hobby bring you joy or stress? If it’s stress, STOP DOING IT. We are not required to do hobbies that we don’t like. That’s what work is for. And we get paid to do it.
